title: The hands nobody sees
told: a sakhi of Guru Amar Das, a traditional story

hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? who did something kind for you this week that you never thanked, maybe never even saw?
options: then this one is for them. listen.
that’s the point of this story. listen.
then listen. i think you’ll find someone.

steps.line: Long ago, an old man named Amar Das walked to the river every morning before dawn, to fill a pitcher of water for his teacher, Guru Angad.
steps.label: a traditional story

steps.line: He carried it a long way back to the village of Khadur, so the Guru could bathe. He did it for years, and never asked for thanks.

steps.q: Nobody made Amar Das do this. Why carry water every single day?
o: He hoped to be chosen as the next Guru
Serving was his way of drawing near to God
He was paid to bring the water
steps.why: For a Sikh, humble service isn’t a chore beside the spiritual life. It is the spiritual life.

steps.line: One stormy night, in the dark and the rain, he tripped beside a weaver’s hut and fell. He kept hold of the pitcher.

steps.q: The noise wakes the weaver’s wife. What do you think she says?
o: That must be homeless old Amru
Who’s there? Come in and get warm
steps.why: She mocked him: homeless old Amru, out in the night with nowhere better to be.

steps.line: Inside, the weaver’s wife grumbled: that must be Amru nithaavan, homeless old Amru, with no place of his own.

steps.q: Word of this reaches Guru Angad. What do you think he does?
o: Tells Amar Das to rest for a while
Turns the insult into an honor
steps.why: He turned it inside out. The man mocked for having no place was honored as a place for others.

steps.line: Guru Angad said: he is not homeless. He is the home of the homeless. In time, he chose Amar Das as the third Guru.

steps.q: Guru Angad chose Amar Das as the next Guru. How old was Amar Das then?
steps.why: He was around seventy-three, older than Guru Angad himself, and he served as Guru for more than twenty years.

steps.line: Today, in gurdwaras everywhere, people still serve like this: shoes handed back, plates scrubbed, roti rolled by someone you’ll never meet.
steps.label: today

steps.line: Sikhs call it seva, selfless service, and name three kinds: with your body, with your mind, and with what you have.
steps.label: today

steps.q: Guru Amar Das made a rule: eat in the langar first, then meet the Guru. Who, tradition says, sat on the floor to eat?
steps.why: Sikh tradition says Akbar sat in the row with everyone else before meeting the Guru. Pangat, sitting in a line on the floor, means no one eats above anyone.

say: here’s what i love. amar das never carried water to be seen. he did it in the dark, for years, and the only one who noticed laughed at him.
that’s seva: service done without ego. in sikh teaching it isn’t a warm-up for the spiritual life. done humbly, it is the practice.

steps.q: Guru Angad had sons of his own, yet he chose the old water-carrier. What was he saying about leading?
o: It’s earned by serving, not inherited
Age matters more than family ties
steps.why: Guru Nanak had done the same, passing over his own sons for Angad. In the line of the Gurus, the one who served was chosen to lead.

today.say: today, do one quiet thing for someone: a dish washed, a message sent, a door held. then tell no one. that’s seva the way amar das did it.
options: then keep it secret. that’s the best part.
look for the one nobody notices. or help in a gurdwara kitchen; anyone is welcome.
